paras: The lynching of Andrew Rainey took place near Bainbridge, Georgia, on the night of April 20, 1903, when a mob took Rainey, a Black man charged with arson, from a constable who was bringing him to jail and beat him so badly that he died the next morning. The officers recognized none of the attackers, and a coroner's inquest failed to learn who they were. An Associated Press dispatch carried the killing to papers in many states, and Black weeklies later counted it among the year's lynchings.

Rainey was suspected of having set fire to the house of Fred Lange, a farmer living thirteen miles from Bainbridge. According to the Associated Press, the fire was set at night while the family was asleep inside. The Savannah Morning News, which spelled the farmer's name "Longe," said only that Rainey was charged with burning the house.

Constable Bell was taking Rainey to Bainbridge to be jailed to await trial on the arson charge. Near the town, at about 8 o'clock in the evening by the Savannah Morning News account, a mob overtook the officer and his prisoner. The Associated Press reported that the mob "demanded the latter under pain of death," and the constable, whom the same dispatch also called "the deputy," gave Rainey up. Rainey was beaten about the body and his skull was fractured.
After the beating he was carried to the jail in Bainbridge, where he died at 6 o'clock the next morning. According to the Savannah Morning News, "the officers failed to recognize any of the mob."

A coroner's inquest was held but did not determine who had beaten Rainey. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a trial appears in the coverage. By summer Rainey's name had entered the running lists of 1903 lynchings, which described him as "colored" and gave his offense as arson.

White newspapers carried the story mainly as a short Associated Press item from Bainbridge dated April 21, under headlines such as "Negro Beaten to Death" and "Negro Beaten by Mob." It ran on April 22 in the Savannah Morning News, the Richmond Times Dispatch, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Indianapolis Journal, while the Minneapolis Journal reduced it to a single line. The Atlanta Constitution printed the same text on April 27, and weeklies in South Carolina, Mississippi, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri and Nevada reprinted or condensed it into early May. None of these white items commented on the killing; they named Rainey's race in the headline and the charge against him in the text.

In the Black press, the Savannah Tribune gave the event one sentence in its April 25 column of news briefs, reporting that Rainey had died in the Bainbridge jail on Tuesday "as the result of a beating administered by a mob," without comment. Later in the year Black weeklies placed the killing in their tallies of mob deaths, all dating it April 23. The Seattle Republican printed its list under the heading "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign" and introduced it as "a pen picture" that Russia and Turkey "might do well to emulate," while the Sedalia Times credited its "Record of Lynching" to The Striker. The same compilation appeared in white papers as well: the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic introduced it with the claim that most victims were "negroes guilty of criminal assault upon white women," and the Indianapolis Journal credited its version to the Providence Journal.

Most reports placed the seizure on the night of April 20, the "last night" of a dispatch dated April 21, and some reprints called it "Monday night." Two printings of the wire text instead said Rainey was taken "this morning," the Keowee Courier redated the dispatch April 24, and the year lists gave April 23. The local Savannah Morning News, with its hour of the attack and of the death, and the Savannah Tribune's report of a Tuesday death both support the night of April 20.
Two Mississippi and Missouri digests said Rainey was "charged with theft" rather than arson, and two others spelled his name "Ramey." Every full account gives the charge as arson.

reader.title: Lynching of Andrew Rainey
bases: A mob took a prisoner charged with arson from a constable and beat him to death (A1, A2).

Rainey died of a beating by a 'mob' that seized him from an officer while he was held on an arson charge (A1, A2); no number is given for the mob, but every report calls it a mob and contemporary year lists counted the death as a lynching (A21, A23).

The Savannah Morning News dispatch, with its own details (time, inquest), and the Associated Press report agree on the seizure, beating and death in jail (A1, A2), and the Black Savannah Tribune reported the death separately (A9); most other white items reprint the AP text.

framing.detail: Short AP item under 'Negro Beaten to Death' or 'Negro Beaten by Mob', with the arson charge in the text and no comment.
Weekly digests reduced it to one sentence, some changing the charge to theft or the name to 'Ramey'.
The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic printed the year list with a preface saying most victims were 'negroes guilty of criminal assault upon white women'.
The Savannah Tribune ran a one-sentence news brief without comment.
The Seattle Republican and Sedalia Times listed the death in tallies of mob killings, the Republican under 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign' with an ironic preface.

versions.value: Night of April 20 ('last night' in an April 21 dispatch; 'Monday night')

conflicts.note: The local Savannah Morning News gives about 8 p.m. the previous night and death at 6 a.m., and the Savannah Tribune gives death on Tuesday (April 21); the 'this morning' variant appears to conflate the seizure with the death, and the April 23 and April 24 dates come from later compilations and a redated reprint.
Only two weekly digests, which share wording, say theft; every full report says arson.
The 'Ramey' spelling appears only in one shared digest item.

record_check.dossier: Supported: seized the night of Monday, April 20; died about 6 a.m. April 21. Variants: 'this morning' (A3, A5), April 23 in year lists, April 24 dateline (A11).
No paper names the county; only Bainbridge, Ga., is given.
Supported (firing the house of Fred Lange, a farmer); two digests say theft.
The papers give the arson charge as the reason he was in custody; no statement from the mob is reported.
4 Black papers: Savannah Tribune brief plus year lists in the Wichita Searchlight, Seattle Republican and Sedalia Times.
At least 19 white papers through 1903-05-02, plus year lists in July.
